hello.note: Casual and fine anywhere. Selamat pagi, siang, sore and malam change with the time of day

good-night.note: At bedtime; literally "safe sleep". Selamat malam (suh-LAH-maht MAH-lahm) is good evening, and also a goodbye at night

goodbye.note: Literally "until we meet". Dah (dah) is a casual bye

please.note: For asking someone to do something: tolong ... Silakan (see-LAH-kahn) is "please, go ahead" when offering

no.note: The final k is a catch in the throat, barely heard. In speech it is often nggak (ng-GAHK)

excuse-me.note: To get past someone or get attention. To apologise, say maaf (mah-AHF)

my-name.note: Saya (I) and Anda (you) are polite and safe for a visitor

speak-slowly.note: Pelan-pelan, slowly: Indonesian often doubles words

speak-english.note: Bisa (can) at the start makes it a question, with the voice rising at the end

ten.note: Se- means one: sepuluh is one ten

thousand.note: Prices are in rupiah: tiga ribu (three thousand) is Rp 3.000

hundred-thousand.note: Written Rp 100.000: Indonesia marks thousands with a dot. Often shortened to 100 rb

million.note: Written Rp 1.000.000, often 1 jt. Sejuta (suh-JOO-tah) also works

how-much.note: Berapa? on its own also works. Point and say Ini berapa? (EE-nee buh-RAH-pah), how much is this?

would-like.note: Literally "I ask for"; the normal polite way to order. The audio uses satu kopi (a coffee) as the example

i-want.note: Direct, and normal everywhere. The audio uses yang ini (this one) as the example

do-you-have.note: Put the item after ada. Ada air? = Do you have water?

discount.note: Literally "can it be less?". Normal in markets, not in malls or minimarkets

card.note: Bayar pakai means pay with. Many places take phone payments by QR code (ris)

bill.note: Ya at the end softens a request. In small eateries people simply ask Bayar di mana? (where do I pay?)

reservation.note: Literally "I have already booked a room"

checkout-time.note: Jam berapa? means what time? for anything

wifi.note: Many people just say password instead of kata sandi

toilet.note: "... di mana?" means "where is ...?" for anything. Signs say Toilet or WC; Pria is men, Wanita women

taxi.note: Most people book rides with an app such as Grab or Gojek

train.note: The full name is kereta api, literally fire carriage

bus.note: Spelled bus, said boos. In many cities the minibuses are called angkot

bus-station.note: The long-distance bus station. A city bus stop is a halte (HAHL-tuh)

which-train.note: Ke means to. Swap in any city; the audio uses Yogyakarta (jog-jah-KAHR-tah) as the example

two-tickets.note: Dua is two; use tiga (3) or empat (4) for more. The audio uses Yogyakarta as the example city
two-tickets.spoken: Bisa beli dua tiket ke Yogyakarta?

trip-length.note: Literally "how long to ...?". The audio uses Yogyakarta as the example city

delicious.note: Enak alone is fine too. Mantap! (MAHN-tahp) is a keen "great!"

allergic.note: Add the food: Saya alergi kacang = I'm allergic to peanuts

love-dish.note: Suka means like; suka sekali, like a lot, is the natural way to say you love food

what-called.note: Point at the dish or item

table-for-two.note: Dua is two. For more people use tiga (3) or empat (4)

menu.note: Boleh means may I. In many small eateries the food is on display instead

recommend.note: Literally "what is good here?", the natural way to ask

beer.note: Bintang is the common local beer. Not every place sells alcohol

coffee.note: Often comes sweet, with the grounds in the cup. Kopi susu has milk

tea.note: Usually sweet. Teh tawar (teh TAH-wahr) is unsweetened, es teh is iced tea

water.note: Air alone means water; air putih (white water) is plain drinking water. Bottled water is air mineral

sugar.note: Tanpa gula (TAHN-pah GOO-lah) means no sugar, worth knowing since drinks come sweet

cheers.note: The standard toast, though often people just raise a glass

help.note: The same word as please when asking a favour
